newsitem.title: CHINA: China's Bao Tong returns home, under surveillance.
newsitem.headline: China's Bao Tong returns home, under surveillance.

text.p: Bao Tong, the most senior Chinese official jailed after 1989 student demonstrations for democracy, has been allowed home after nearly a year of house arrest and seven years in jail, his family said on Wednesday.

But Bao, 64, former secretary to Zhao Ziyang who was toppled as Communist Party chief after the military crushed the 1989 demonstrations and who was privy to the Communist Party's innermost secrets, remained under tight police surveillance.
"My father is happy because it feels like he is at home now," his daughter, Bao Jian, said by telephone.
"It remains to be seen how much freedom (he) will have in future," his son, Bao Puliu, said by telephone from the United States.
A source close to the family said surveillance had been tight since Bao Tong, his wife, daughter and grand-daughter moved into a new third-floor flat in Shijingshan in western Beijing last Saturday.
"When he goes out, security agents follow him around," said the source who asked not to be identified. "They're at the front door downstairs. They're in the yard."

Bao Tong spent 11 months under virtual house arrest in a rundown state dormitory in the Western Hills outside Beijing after completing in May 1996 a seven-year jail term for his role in the 1989 demonstrations.
He had been convicted of leaking state secrets -- apparently passing information that notified students that the government planned to impose martial law in Beijing in late May 1989.

He was allowed to return home only after his family agreed to give up their former comfortable government-allocated home intended for senior officials in central Beijing and to move to Shijingshan, about 10 km (6.2 miles) further west.
"Bao Tong is being shunted to Shijingshan to make it easier to control him," a second source close to the family said.

Diplomats say Bao Tong is a source of anxiety for China's leaders, who fear he may reveal details of the dealings of the highest party and government echelons in the weeks before the bloody June 4, 1989, crackdown on demonstrators.
"The apartment building is brand new...making surveillance very convenient," the source said.
"Security agents could be his neighbours," the source said.
The second and fourth floors of the six-storey building were unoccupied. The Baos have the entire third floor to themselves, occupying about 85 square metres (915 square ft), but have no telephone.
Bao Tong is barred from meeting foreign reporters because of a two-year suspension of his political rights that ends in May 1998.

His health was not good but he was in high spirits, his family said. Bao Tong was treated for a variety of ailments while in prison, including jaw and neck ailments and intestinal polyps that required six operations.

He held ministerial status when he was secretary to the Communist Party's powerful Politburo Standing Committee in the late 1980s, making him the most senior official to be jailed after the 1989 demonstrations.
Placing Bao under virtual house arrest had drawn fire from the United States, which protested against his detention without recourse to judicial representation and access to his family.
Chinese officials had defended Bao's detention, saying the measures were necessary and required by law.
